propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of May 26, 2021 decision refusing permanent residence on H&C grounds.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Sathiyarajah Amarasingam, seeks judicial review, pursuant to section 72 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], of a decision dated May 26, 2021, of a Senior Immigration Officer [the Officer] refusing the Applicant’s application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate [H&C] grounds.

propositions.text: Applicant argues the decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: On judicial review, the Applicant argues that the decision is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of May 26, 2021 refusal of permanent residence on H&C grounds and argues decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is allowed and matter remitted to different officer for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, the application for judicial review is allowed. The matter is remitted to a different immigration officer for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows judicial review and remits matter to different officer for reconsideration.

propositions.text: Applicant is 52-year-old Sri Lankan citizen who entered Canada in 2011 and claimed refugee status as Tamil Hindu minority member.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a 52-year-old citizen of Sri Lanka. He entered Canada on January 7, 2011, and made a refugee claim on the basis that he was being persecuted as a member of a minority community in Sri Lanka, the Tamil Hindu.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant is 52-year-old Sri Lankan citizen who claimed refugee status as Tamil Hindu minority member in 2011.

propositions.text: Applicant was detained and persecuted during Sri Lankan civil war and faced harassment in government-controlled territory due to suspected LTTE association.
propositions.quote: As a youth and young man, during the civil war in Sri Lanka, the Applicant was allegedly detained and exposed to various persecutions. He and his family left the part of the country that was controlled by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam [LTTE], a militant secessionist organization, and began living in the government-controlled territory. There, he continued to face harassment, mob attacks, extortion, and robbery, on the suspicion that he was associated with the LTTE.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant was detained and persecuted during civil war and faced harassment due to suspected LTTE association, per earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Refugee claim refused March 26, 2012, as attacks deemed criminal and risk generalized; judicial review leave denied August 15, 2012.
propositions.quote: On March 26, 2012, his refugee claim was refused on the basis that the motivation for the attacks and extortion were criminal in nature and that the threat of future extortion or kidnapping was a generalized risk faced by others in the country. He sought leave for judicial review of the decision, but his application was denied on August 15, 2012.

paragraphs.summary: Refugee claim refused in 2012 as attacks were criminal and risk generalized; judicial review leave denied.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for permanent residence on H&C grounds June 21, 2012, refused June 24, 2013; removal order issued December 23, 2012; Applicant did not appear due to fear.
propositions.quote: On June 21, 2012, he submitted an application for permanent residence on H&C grounds, which was also refused on June 24, 2013. An order for removal was issued against him to leave Canada on December 23, 2012. The Applicant did not appear for his removal because of his alleged continued fear to return to Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's H&C application refused; removal order issued but Applicant did not appear due to fear of return.

propositions.text: Warrant issued December 27, 2012; Applicant remained and worked without authorization; warrant executed August 20, 2020; released with conditions.
propositions.quote: On December 27, 2012, a warrant was issued against him. However, he continued to remain and work in Canada without authorization for an extended period of time. The warrant against him was executed on August 20, 2020, and he was released with conditions.

paragraphs.summary: Warrant issued in 2012; Applicant stayed and worked without authorization; warrant executed in 2020; released with conditions.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted second H&C application August 19, 2020, citing establishment, children's best interests, and adverse country conditions.
propositions.quote: Upon the execution of the warrant, on August 19, 2020, the Applicant submitted a second application for permanent residence based on H&C grounds. The motives for this application were his level of establishment in Canada, the best interest of the children, and the adverse country conditions in Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submitted second H&C application in 2020 citing establishment, children's interests, and adverse country conditions.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted Pre-Removal Risk Assessment application March 16, 2021.
propositions.quote: On March 16, 2021, he submitted a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment [PRRA] application.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submitted PRRA application in March 2021.

propositions.text: H&C application and PRRA refused May 26, 2021; Officer not satisfied humanitarian considerations justified exemption under IRPA.
propositions.quote: After conducting a global assessment of all the factors raised by the Applicant, the H&C application was denied on May 26, 2021. The Applicant’s PRRA decision was also refused at the same time by the same Officer. The Officer was not satisfied that the humanitarian and compassionate considerations justified an exemption under subsection 25(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: H&C and PRRA applications refused May 26, 2021; Officer found humanitarian considerations did not justify exemption.

propositions.text: Applicant had some establishment in Canada but remained and worked without authorization and failed to appear for removal, going underground for over eight years.
propositions.quote: With regards to the criterion of establishment, the Officer concluded that the Applicant had a degree of establishment in Canada. Nevertheless, the Officer also noted that the Applicant continued to remain and work in Canada without authorization for a prolonged period. The Officer also considered that the Applicant had failed to appear for removal on December 23, 2012, and had subsequently gone underground for more than eight years.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant had some establishment but remained unauthorized and went underground over eight years.

propositions.text: Applicant showed disregard for Canadian regulations by not regularizing status until recently, negatively affecting application.
propositions.quote: Because the Applicant did not make further attempts to regularize his status in Canada during that period, until recently, the Officer found that the Applicant had shown disregard for Canadian regulations and that this failure negatively affected his application.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant's failure to regularize status showed disregard for regulations and hurt application.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that Applicant would be discriminated or mistreated as Tamil returnee or long-term resident in Sri Lanka.
propositions.quote: With regards to the risks and adverse country conditions, the Officer concluded that there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Applicant would, on a balance of probabilities, be discriminated against or mistreated simply as a result of his status as a Tamil returnee and also as a person who had resided in Canada for the past decade.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found insufficient evidence Applicant would be discriminated or mistreated in Sri Lanka as Tamil returnee or long-term resident.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to provide sufficient corroborative evidence of past mistreatment by army or paramilitary; no evidence of ongoing threat in Sri Lanka.
propositions.quote: More specifically regarding the forward-looking hardships that the Applicant would face upon his return to Sri Lanka, the Officer found that the Applicant did not provide sufficient corroborative evidence of past mistreatment or abuse at the hands of the army or People’s Liberation Organisation of Tamil Eelam, a pro-government paramilitary group supporting the LTTE. The Officer further noted that the Applicant resided in Canada for over ten years and had not objectively established with sufficient evidence that anyone in Sri Lanka had an ongoing interest to locate and harm him.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant lacked corroborative evidence of past mistreatment or ongoing threat in Sri Lanka.

propositions.text: Evidence shows only politically active individuals likely detained; Applicant not politically active or perceived as LTTE sympathizer.
propositions.quote: The Officer also relied on documentary evidence indicating that those who are likely to be detained and interrogated upon return are individuals with a history of significant political activity, which the Applicant had not established. The Officer found that the Applicant had presented insufficient evidence to demonstrate that anyone in Sri Lanka perceives or would perceive him to be related to the LTTE supporter or sympathizers.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found only politically active detained; Applicant not politically active or perceived as LTTE sympathizer.

propositions.text: Discrimination against Tamils exists but Applicant did not show hardship level justifying exemption; family not denied social services.
propositions.quote: The Officer also noted that while discrimination against Tamils is clearly present in Sri Lanka, the Applicant had not demonstrated that he would face a level of hardship that would justify an exemption from legislative requirements (H&C considerations). In fact, the Officer noted that insufficient evidence had been provided to show that the Applicant’s family members who still reside in Visuvamadu in the Northern Province of Sri Lanka were denied access to education, employment, health services, or other social services.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found discrimination exists but Applicant did not show hardship justifying exemption; family not denied services.

propositions.text: Applicant is resilient, can adapt on return with family support; Canadian skills transferable in Sri Lanka.
propositions.quote: The Officer further found that the Applicant is a resilient individual who will be able to adapt upon his return to Sri Lanka as his family members will be able to support him financially. The skills he obtained as an assembler, general labourer, and maintenance worker in Canada will also be transferrable for him in Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant resilient, able to adapt with family support; skills transferable in Sri Lanka.

propositions.text: Determinative issue is whether Officer's refusal of H&C application was reasonable.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this judicial review is whether the Officer’s decision to refuse the H&C application was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies issue as reasonableness of Officer's refusal of H&C application.

propositions.text: Standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov: decision must be coherent, rational, justified by facts and law.
propositions.quote: The applicable standard of review is one of reasonableness as set out in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov]. A reasonable decision “is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov at para 85).

paragraphs.summary: Court states standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov requiring coherent, rational, justified decision.

propositions.text: Court may intervene if decision has serious shortcomings beyond superficial, lacking justification, intelligibility, transparency.
propositions.quote: For the reviewing court to intervene, the challenging party must satisfy the court that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency”, and that such alleged shortcomings or flaws are “more than merely superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision” (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: Court may intervene if decision has serious, non-superficial shortcomings lacking justification, intelligibility, transparency.

propositions.text: The decision ignores relevant evidence and applies illogical reasoning, making it neither justifiable nor intelligible.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that because the decision ignores relevant evidence and applies illogical reasoning, it is neither justifiable nor intelligible (Vavilov at paras 104, 126).

propositions.text: Reasonableness may be jeopardized if decision maker misapprehended or failed to account for evidence, or if reasons show clear logical fallacies.
propositions.quote: “the reasonableness of a decision may be jeopardized where the decision maker has fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it” and “the internal rationality of a decision may be called into question if the reasons exhibit clear logical fallacies, such as circular reasoning, false dilemmas, unfounded generalizations or an absurd premise” (Vavilov at para 104).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues decision ignores evidence and is illogical; Vavilov sets reasonableness standards for decision-making.

propositions.text: Decision maker cannot selectively choose evidence and ignore contradicting facts; must consider and weigh all evidence and explain contrary evidence.
propositions.quote: a decision maker cannot selectively choose evidence and ignore contradicting facts. Instead, the decision maker must demonstrate that all of the evidence was considered and weighed, as well as explain why evidence that would be contrary to the result was not sufficient to justify a different conclusion

propositions.text: Intervening is appropriate when decision maker did not properly mention contradicting facts and court cannot assess meaningful consideration of key issues.
propositions.quote: intervening because the decision maker did not properly mention contradicting facts is appropriate when the Court cannot assess whether the decision maker meaningfully considered all of the key issues and evidence

propositions.text: Overturning a decision for not discussing critical contradicting evidence is not disguised correctness but shows failure to consider relevant evidence or argument.
propositions.quote: Overturning a decision because the reasons did not discuss critical contradicting evidence is not “disguised correctness” - nor the application of a court established “yardstick” to measure the decision maker’s reasons

paragraphs.summary: Court explains decision makers must consider all evidence and explain contrary evidence; failure to do so justifies intervention.

propositions.text: Officer turned positive H&C factors into negative ones, contrary to jurisprudence.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the Decision is unreasonable because the Officer turned positive H&C factors into negative ones, contrary to the rule established by jurisprudence.

propositions.text: Officer used Applicant's resilience to justify conclusion he could adapt to home country, which is unreasonable per Singh.
propositions.quote: despite noting the discrimination the Applicant might face, the Officer points to his resilience as a way to justify his conclusion that “he will be able to adapt to the environment of his home country after an initial period of adjustment.” In Singh v Canada ... this Court found such reasoning unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer unreasonably turned positive factors negative, citing Singh case.

propositions.text: Officer ignored relevant evidence contradicting decision that Applicant failed to show risk if removed after over ten years.
propositions.quote: the Officer ignored relevant evidence that contradicted their decision that the Applicant was unable to demonstrate a risk if removed, on a balance of probabilities and more than ten years after having left Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant contends Officer ignored evidence contradicting risk assessment after long absence.

propositions.text: Same Officer decided PRRA and H&C applications on same record but excluded relevant PRRA analysis from H&C decision.
propositions.quote: the Officer deciding the H&C application in this case was the same Officer that was also considering the PRRA application, and both decisions rested on the exact same record. However, despite copying the PRRA analysis into the H&C decision, the Officer excluded the sections of the PRRA analysis that were in fact more relevant to an H&C analysis.

propositions.text: PRRA analysis cited evidence of increased military presence and harassment of Tamils, but these were omitted from H&C decision.
propositions.quote: in the PRRA analysis ... the decision maker cited a source from Freedom House in 2019 indicating that military presence increased in Tamil-populated areas and that the government encouraged settlement with the aim of diluting local Tamil majorities. The decision maker also cited a US Department of State Report of 2020 in which Tamils are reporting events of harassment at the hands of security forces.

propositions.text: PRRA analysis concluded human rights abuses against Tamils may not have been fully addressed and discrimination may continue.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence I have consulted demonstrates that human rights abuses committed in the past in Sri Lanka may still not have been fully addressed by the government. Tamils may continue to face discrimination due to their ethnicity.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant notes Officer excluded relevant PRRA evidence of discrimination and harassment from H&C decision.

propositions.text: Officer either misunderstood differences between PRRA and H&C tests or improperly excluded positive information from H&C decision.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the Officer either did not properly appreciate the differences between the PRRA and H&C tests, or simply improperly excluded information from the H&C decision that should have been given positive weight.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer misunderstood or improperly excluded relevant evidence in H&C decision.

propositions.text: Officer gave no weight to evidence of discrimination and applied PRRA risk analysis to H&C, ignoring different criteria.
propositions.quote: the Officer gave no weight to the available evidence of discrimination against Tamils, opting instead to repeat the risk analysis of the PRRA. In doing so, the Officer applied the same legal requirements, despite the fact that the criteria are different for the H&C test.

propositions.text: Officer failed to consider relevant factors through humanitarian and compassionate lens, dismissing evidence of discrimination and adverse conditions.
propositions.quote: the Officer failed to consider relevant factors through a humanitarian and compassionate lens. Overall, by applying the more onerous PRRA standards and dismissing relevant evidence of discrimination, militarization, and adverse country conditions that will directly impact the Applicant, the Officer failed to consider relevant factors otherwise necessary under the H&C lens.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits Officer wrongly applied PRRA standards to H&C, ignoring relevant humanitarian factors.

propositions.text: Officer considered whether discrimination amounted to hardship justifying positive H&C, finding insufficient evidence of family hardship.
propositions.quote: the Respondent submits that the Officer turned their mind to whether the level of discrimination faced by the Applicant amounted to a hardship that justified a positive H&C, finding that there was insufficient evidence that his family in Sri Lanka was facing difficulties and that they could help him settle upon his return.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Officer reasonably assessed discrimination and family hardship for H&C.

propositions.text: Officer's overall assessment was reasonable; evidence of discrimination against family did not amount to hardship warranting H&C relief.
propositions.quote: the Respondent further submits that the Officer’s overall assessment was reasonable based on the evidence that was before them. The Officer considered the evidence of discrimination against similarly situated individuals, such as the Applicant’s family in Sri Lanka, and found that it did not amount to hardship.

propositions.text: Officer could consider current situation of Applicant’s family and find it did not warrant H&C relief.
propositions.quote: In this case, it was open to the Officer to look at what the current situation for the Applicant’s family was at the time of evaluation, and find that it didn’t rise to the level where H&C relief was warranted.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits Officer reasonably found family situation did not justify H&C relief.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably considered Applicant’s establishment factors independently and gave them negative weight in context of immigration history.
propositions.quote: With respect to the argument on the positive factors that were used against the Applicant, the Respondent argues that the Officer reasonably considered the Applicant’s establishment factors independently from the assessment of the hardship in Sri Lanka and gave it negative weight within the context of his whole immigration history.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Officer reasonably gave negative weight to establishment factors in context.

propositions.text: Subsection 25(1) IRPA gives Minister discretion to grant permanent residence for humanitarian and compassionate reasons.
propositions.quote: Subsection 25(1) of the IRPA provides the Minister with the discretionary power to exempt a foreigner from having to meet any criteria or obligation of the IRPA and to grant him/her permanent resident status, if the Minister is of the opinion that it is justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations.

propositions.text: Section 25(1) IRPA text provides Minister may grant permanent residence if justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations, considering best interests of affected child.
propositions.quote: Subject to subsection (1.2), the Minister must, on request of a foreign national in Canada who applies for permanent resident status ... may grant the foreign national permanent resident status ... if the Minister is of the opinion that it is justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations relating to the foreign national, taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected.

paragraphs.summary: Court states IRPA s.25(1) grants Minister discretion to grant permanent residence for humanitarian and compassionate reasons.

propositions.text: Applicants bear onus to satisfy decision maker that permanent residence or exemption is justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
propositions.quote: applicants who apply for H&C considerations bear the onus of satisfying the decision maker that the granting of permanent resident status or an exemption ... is justified by H&C considerations

propositions.text: Cites Lee, Owusu, Prasad, Patel cases supporting onus on applicant for H&C relief.
propositions.quote: Lee v Canada ... citing Owusu ... citing Prasad ... and Patel ...

paragraphs.summary: Court explains applicants bear onus to prove humanitarian and compassionate justification for relief.

propositions.text: Test for H&C relief requires exceptional circumstances causing misfortunes greater than typical applicants, citing Huang and Kanthasamy.
propositions.quote: The test for H&C relief is set out in Huang ... Section 25 of the IRPA provides exceptional relief ... applicants must demonstrate misfortunes or other H&C considerations that are greater than those typically faced by others ... Kanthasamy ...

propositions.text: Applicants must establish exceptional reasons to be allowed to remain or obtain H&C relief, citing Chieu, Jesuthasan, Kanguatjivi.
propositions.quote: applicants for H&C relief must “establish exceptional reasons as to why they should be allowed to remain in Canada” ... Chieu ... Jesuthasan ... Kanguatjivi ...

propositions.text: All relevant facts and factors advanced by applicant must be considered and weighed in H&C assessment.
propositions.quote: In assessing whether an applicant has established sufficient H&C considerations ... all of the relevant facts and factors advanced by the applicant must be considered and weighed: Kanthasamy

paragraphs.summary: Court outlines H&C relief test requires exceptional circumstances and weighing all relevant factors.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy holds applicant need only show likely discrimination, which may be inferred from group membership.
propositions.quote: the Supreme Court of Canada held that the applicant only needs to show that it is likely that discrimination will occur, and that such a conclusion may be inferred

propositions.text: Discrimination can be inferred from membership in discriminated group; direct evidence of personal targeting not required.
propositions.quote: Discrimination for the purpose of humanitarian and compassionate applications “could manifest in isolated incidents or permeate systemically”, and even “[a] series of discriminatory events that do not give rise to persecution must be considered cumulatively” ... reasonable inferences can be drawn from those experiences.

propositions.text: Officer erred by requiring direct evidence of personal targeting, undermining humanitarian purpose of s.25(1).
propositions.quote: the Officer required Jeyakannan Kanthasamy to present direct evidence that he would face such a risk of discrimination if deported. This not only undermines the humanitarian purpose of s. 25(1), it reflects an anemic view of discrimination

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy holds discrimination risk may be inferred from group membership; requiring direct evidence is error.

propositions.text: Respondent cites Shackleford and Kanthasamy to argue H&C relief should only be granted in exceptional circumstances to avoid becoming alternative immigration scheme.
propositions.quote: the Respondent cited Shackleford ... relying on Kanthasamy ... in which the Court opined that an H&C application should only be granted in exceptional circumstances. Otherwise, section 25 would risk becoming the alternative immigration scheme

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues H&C relief must be exceptional to avoid misuse, citing Shackleford and Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: Officer unreasonably turned positive H&C establishment factors into negative ones against Applicant.
propositions.quote: the Applicant’s argument that the Officer turned positive H&C establishment factors into negative ones should be sustained.

propositions.text: Officer noted Applicant's resilience and work skills but used these to conclude Applicant could adapt to Sri Lanka, which is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the Officer noted that the Applicant was “resilient” and had obtained “work skills in Canada that could be transferrable in Sri Lanka”. Instead of considering those factors as relevant to his H&C application, the Officer instead opined that this demonstrated that the Applicant could re-establish in Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer unreasonably used positive factors against Applicant to conclude he could adapt to Sri Lanka.

propositions.text: Respondent argues Officer reasonably considered establishment factors negatively in context of immigration history and hardship in Sri Lanka.
propositions.quote: the Respondent submits that the Officer reasonably considered the establishment factors independently and gave it a negative weight within the context of the Applicant’s past immigration history and in the context of considering hardship in Sri Lanka.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Respondent's argument that Officer's negative weighting of establishment factors was reasonable.
propositions.quote: I disagree.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent defends Officer's negative weighting of establishment factors; Court disagrees.

propositions.text: Officer cannot turn positive establishment factors into negative ones; using positive skills against applicants is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the Officer is not allowed to turn positive establishment factors into negative ones ... To turn positive establishment factors on their head is unreasonable. The officer cannot ... use the Applicants’ shield against them as a sword.

propositions.text: Cites Singh, Sosi, Lauture cases criticizing use of positive establishment factors to deny H&C relief.
propositions.quote: As this Court held in Singh ... The Court found against the officer’s statement ... Sosi ... Lauture ...

propositions.text: Officer committed error by using positive establishment skills to detriment in hardship and BIOC analysis.
propositions.quote: the Officer committed this error by applauding the Applicants’ successful ability to assimilate ... but then using those positive skills to their detriment ... And the Officer committed a further unreasonable error in using similar logic in the BIOC analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Officer erred by using positive establishment factors negatively, citing precedent cases.

propositions.text: Court agrees Officer unreasonably turned positive establishment factors against Applicant, making conclusion unintelligible.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant that the Officer unreasonably turned positive establishment factors on their head ... This conclusion is unintelligible

propositions.text: Cites Teweldemedhn, Li, Lauture cases supporting that turning positive factors against applicant is unintelligible.
propositions.quote: see also Teweldemedhn ... Li ... Lauture ...

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees Officer's reasoning is unintelligible and cites supporting cases.

propositions.text: Officers deciding PRRA and H&C applications simultaneously risk confusing distinct analyses and must keep processes separate.
propositions.quote: officers who rule on both types of applications at the same time are “at risk of confusing the two separate and distinct analyses required by these procedures… and may be drawn to the same conclusion [and therefore] extra care should be taken to ensure the two processes are kept separate.”

propositions.text: Cites Ramirez case warning about risk of conflating PRRA and H&C analyses when decided together.
propositions.quote: As held by this Court in Ramirez ... officers who rule on both types of applications at the same time are “at risk of confusing the two separate and distinct analyses required by these procedures…

paragraphs.summary: Court warns Officers deciding PRRA and H&C together risk conflating analyses and must keep them separate.

propositions.text: The Officer considered some evidence in PRRA but ignored relevant contradictory evidence in the H&C decision.
propositions.quote: the Officer considered some evidentiary elements in making their findings on the PRRA application, but then ignored some of the same relevant evidence in the H&C decision

propositions.text: The evidence ignored in the H&C decision contradicts the Officer's finding.
propositions.quote: the evidence that was ignored for the purposes of the H&C decision is directly in contradiction to their finding

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer considered evidence in PRRA but ignored contradictory evidence in the H&C decision, which contradicts the Officer's finding.

propositions.text: Omission to consider relevant contradictory evidence is unreasonable (Vavilov at para 128).
propositions.quote: the omission to consider relevant objective evidence that is contradictory to the findings is unreasonable (Vavilov at para 128)

propositions.text: Decision maker cannot cherry-pick evidence fitting rationale and ignore contradictory evidence.
propositions.quote: The decision maker is not allowed to choose the evidence that fits its rationale, but ignore existing evidence that point to a contradictory conclusion

propositions.text: Decision maker must explain why contradicting evidence was given little or no weight and why application was dismissed despite it (Ehigiator at para 74; Rajput at para 25).
propositions.quote: the decision maker must explain why little or no weight had to be assigned to the contradicting evidence and why it preferred, in light of the contradicting evidence, to dismiss the application (Ehigiator at para 74; Rajput v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 65 at para 25)

paragraphs.summary: The court states the law that ignoring contradictory evidence without explanation is unreasonable, citing Vavilov, Ehigiator, and Rajput.

propositions.text: Applicant provided evidence of growing discrimination against Tamils in Sri Lanka and his membership in that group.
propositions.quote: the Applicant provided documentary evidence showing that Tamils were facing growing discrimination in Sri Lanka today and that he was part of this group

propositions.text: The Officer considered that evidence but failed to consider it fully in the H&C analysis.
propositions.quote: The Officer considered that evidence, but failed to consider it entirely for the purposes of the H&C analysis

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicant provided evidence of Tamil discrimination, which the Officer considered but did not fully consider in the H&C analysis.

propositions.text: The Officer had a complete record and considered discrimination evidence in PRRA but excluded it from H&C analysis.
propositions.quote: The Officer had a complete record and did consider the evidence relating to the discrimination and harassment of Tamils as well as concerns that the government had not fully addressed the situation. While that information was considered in the PRRA analysis, it was excluded from the H&C analysis

propositions.text: The discrimination evidence was relevant and should have been considered in the H&C decision, but the Officer failed to do so.
propositions.quote: that information remained relevant and ought to have been considered and analyzed in the H&C decision. The Officer failed to do so

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer considered discrimination evidence in PRRA but wrongly excluded it from the relevant H&C decision.

propositions.text: The Officer either failed to appreciate PRRA and H&C differences or failed to weigh contradicting evidence.
propositions.quote: The Officer either failed to appreciate the differences between the PRRA test and the H&C criteria, or failed to consider and weigh contradicting evidence

propositions.text: The Officer's reasons do not explain why important evidence was disregarded in decision-making.
propositions.quote: the reasons do not provide an explanation as to why that important evidence played no role in the Officer’s decision-making process

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer failed to appreciate test differences or weigh evidence and gave no explanation for ignoring important evidence.

propositions.text: Discrimination, harassment, or threats may impact the Applicant if removed and are important in H&C process even if not meeting PRRA test.
propositions.quote: issues as to potential discrimination, harassment, or threats of criminal violence, even if they don’t meet the PRRA test, may directly impact the Applicant if he is removed. Those are important considerations in the H&C process

paragraphs.summary: The court states that discrimination and threats, even if not meeting PRRA test, are important in H&C considerations.

propositions.text: The correct legal test for H&C is broader than strict hardship, considering humanitarian factors responsive to case facts (Kanthasamy at para 25).
propositions.quote: The correct legal test is not a strict hardships lens, but a broader one that considers the humanitarian and compassionate factors that is responsive to the facts of the case (Kanthasamy at para 25)

propositions.text: The Officer failed to apply the correct legal test and erred.
propositions.quote: The Officer failed to do so, and thus erred by applying an incorrect legal test

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer erred by applying an incorrect legal test, which should be broader and humanitarian-focused.

propositions.text: The Officer did not rely on the most up-to-date evidence relevant to H&C assessment.
propositions.quote: the Officer did not appear to rely on the most up-to-date evidence that was relevant to the H&C assessment

propositions.text: Sri Lanka's situation is fluid; Officer should have relied on recent objective evidence like UNHCR Guidelines.
propositions.quote: in the circumstances of this case where Sri Lanka is a country in which the situation is fluid, the Officer was able to and should have relied on the most recent objective evidence (more specifically the UNHCR Eligibility Guidelines)

propositions.text: Justice Brown in Krishnapillai emphasized need for timely, up-to-date PRRA assessment based on current country conditions.
propositions.quote: To the extent reasonably possible, a PRRA should be based on up-to-date country condition evidence

propositions.text: Justice Brown noted Sri Lanka's situation is fluid and PRRA decisions must consider recent evidence.
propositions.quote: it seems to me the situation in Sri Lanka is once again fluid, which emphasizes the need for timely and up-to-date PRRA assessment

propositions.text: Justice Favel in Navaratnam held failure to consider recent country condition evidence renders decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Where a decision maker fails to consider recent country condition evidence and bases a risk conclusion on outdated country conditions, such decision is unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer failed to rely on up-to-date evidence; cites authorities emphasizing need for timely, current country condition evidence.

propositions.text: The decision lacks intelligibility and is not reasonable.
propositions.quote: the decision lacks intelligibility and is therefore not reasonable

propositions.text: Judicial review application is granted and matter remitted for redetermination by a different officer.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is granted. The matter is remitted for redetermination by a different officer

propositions.text: No questions for certification were argued or arise.
propositions.quote: No questions for certification were argued, and I agree none arise

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review, remits matter for redetermination by a different officer, and finds no certification questions.
